case_study_insert.main_stem: Velvet Vale Boutiques (VVB) is a private limited company in the fashion retail sector, operating a chain of six women's clothing boutiques and employing a workforce of 40. Founded in 2013 by Elena Vale, the business has a hierarchical organisational structure with autocratic leadership. VVB plans to invest $560,000 in refurbishing three boutiques and launching an online store, financed by a $200,000 bank loan and a $360,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $240,000 a year, a variable cost of $18 a unit and a selling price of $48, and produces 20,000 units a year. VVB faces labour turnover of 14% among sales assistants and a rising number of complaints about out-of-stock sizes in its boutiques.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Boutique Operations Report — Q4 2025: VVB sold 5,400 garments across its six boutiques last quarter, with labour turnover of 14% among sales assistants and 38 customer complaints about unavailable sizes, up from 22 a year earlier. Average queueing time at tills was 6 minutes, and 91% of planned deliveries arrived on time. A survey of 900 shoppers found 58% preferred shops with knowledgeable staff and 49% would use an online store. A skills audit shows 11 of 40 staff have not completed on-the-job training; off-the-job training at the regional college costs $620 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Velvet Vale Boutiques as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Retail Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.0%, increasing the cost of VVB's $200,000 bank loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.4% from $13.10 to $13.94 an hour from April 2026, raising the wages of sales assistants. (3) Wholesale clothing input costs have risen 10.8% year-on-year, while consumer spending on fashion rose 2.6%.

questions.question_text: VVB is funding its $560,000 expansion with a $200,000 bank loan and a $360,000 share issue. Explain two advantages for VVB of the share issue compared with the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A share issue brings in $360,000 that never has to be repaid and carries no regular interest charge, unlike the $200,000 bank loan whose cost rises whenever the base rate moves. For a firm with fixed costs of $240,000 a year and stock problems, this protects cash flow while three boutiques are refurbished, leaving more of the $48 selling price to cover the $18 variable cost and absorb the 10.8% rise in wholesale clothing costs.

Point 2: Equity does not require the collateral or monthly repayment pressure of a bank loan, so Elena Vale's expansion cannot be threatened by a bank recall if sales disappoint during the launch of the new online store. Although a share issue dilutes existing ownership, it spreads the funding burden among investors rather than concentrating risk on one lender, and it supports the $560,000 project without committing the boutiques' limited cash reserves. That matters when labour turnover of 14% and 38 complaints about unavailable sizes already strain the workforce of 40 and require spending on staff and stock before the refurbished boutiques generate extra revenue.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to VVB's expansion financing.

questions.question_text: VVB wants to attract shoppers to its new online store. Consider national television advertising, local newspaper advertising, or social media influencer marketing. Which should VVB choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National television advertising: Television could build brand awareness for the six boutiques and the new online store across the whole country, reinforcing the 58% of 900 surveyed shoppers who prefer knowledgeable staff. However, airtime is expensive for a business with $240,000 fixed costs and a $200,000 bank loan, and most viewers live outside VVB's physical catchment; much of the spend would be wasted on viewers who never buy women's clothing from this chain.

Local newspaper advertising: Newspaper adverts are cheaper and can target the towns around the six boutiques, with vouchers that drive immediate visits and help clear the stock behind 38 complaints about unavailable sizes. Their limits are falling readership and a static image that cannot show the clothing or explain the new online store, so they do little to reach the 49% of surveyed shoppers who said they would use online shopping.

Social media influencer marketing: Fashion influencers can model the garments, show the refurbished boutiques and direct followers to the online store, reaching the 49% who would shop online and the 58% who value expert advice. Engagement is measurable against the 5,400-garment quarterly baseline and the 38 complaints. Drawbacks are that fees can be high, results build gradually, and credibility depends on choosing reviewers who genuinely fit VVB's brand.

Recommendation: VVB should choose social media influencer marketing, with small local newspaper vouchers for the refurbishment launch week. It displays the product, reaches online shoppers that newspapers cannot, and costs far less than television for a $560,000 expansion partly funded by debt. Television is rejected as unaffordable and poorly targeted, and newspapers are rejected as the main channel because they cannot demonstrate the clothing or sell the online store. A phased influencer campaign lets Elena Vale track sales against the 5,400 baseline before committing more budget.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal application to VVB.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of VVB with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in context with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and newspapers are rejected.

questions.question_text: VVB's labour turnover is 14% and complaints about out-of-stock sizes are rising under autocratic leadership. Explain two benefits for VVB of adopting a more democratic leadership style.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership would let the workforce of 40, especially sales assistants, suggest how to manage stock and request missing sizes. Being consulted raises job satisfaction and commitment, which should reduce the 14% labour turnover that forces VVB to recruit and retrain repeatedly; experienced assistants who stay are better placed to prevent the 38 complaints about unavailable sizes.

Point 2: Staff on the shop floor see firsthand which sizes sell out and which deliveries arrive late, so involving them improves decisions on ordering and display, addressing the 38 complaints and protecting the 91% on-time delivery record. Higher morale also supports the 58% of 900 surveyed shoppers who prefer knowledgeable staff: engaged, longer-serving assistants give better advice, strengthening the boutiques' reputation as the $560,000 refurbishment and new online store are launched. Moving away from autocratic leadership also fits the change programme Elena Vale needs to reduce disruption among the workforce of 40.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to VVB's turnover, complaints, structure and expansion.

questions.question_text: VVB must train 11 of 40 staff who have not completed on-the-job training. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the regional college. Which should VVB choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching on the shop floor is tailored to VVB's own stock system and customer-service standards, costs no course fees, and keeps the 11 trainees productive during the 5,400-garment quarter. Supervisors can correct the mistakes behind 38 complaints about unavailable sizes immediately and coach assistants on advising the 58% of shoppers who value knowledgeable staff. The weaknesses are that busy senior staff have less time to teach, bad habits can spread, and there is no external certificate to evidence competence.

Off-the-job training: The regional college course at $620 per employee costs 11 × $620 = $6,820, small beside the $560,000 investment. It offers structured retail skills and a recognised certificate, useful as VVB opens an online store and refurbishes three boutiques. However, it removes 11 of a workforce of 40 from the shops during trading, which could worsen the 38 complaints and lengthen the 6-minute till queues, and generic content must still be adapted to VVB's own stock system.

Decision: VVB should choose on-the-job training first, backed by short certified college modules for senior assistants. It is cheaper, specific to the boutiques and avoids disrupting service while 14% labour turnover is already stretching a workforce of 40. Full off-the-job training is rejected now because $6,820 and eleven lost shifts would hit the 5,400-garment operation and the launch timetable. Elena Vale should trial the approach in one boutique, then compare the 38 complaints and the 91% delivery record before extending it, only paying the $620 fee later where formal certification is needed.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to VVB.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of both training methods in the context of VVB.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods with a well-justified decision covering cost, service disruption and relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how VVB's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $240,000 ÷ ($48 − $18) = $240,000 ÷ $30 = 8,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 8,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $48 − $18 = $30. Answer: contribution per unit is $30.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways VVB's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Comparing the 8,000-unit break-even point with output of 20,000 units gives a margin of safety of 12,000 units, showing the fall in demand the six boutiques and new online store could absorb before losses begin.
2. Contribution per unit of $30 lets managers test discounts: cutting the $48 price by $3 to $45 leaves $27 contribution, so they can judge whether extra sales from the 49% who would use the online store compensate for the lower margin.
3. With a $200,000 bank loan to service and a $560,000 refurbishment underway, the $30 contribution and 20,000-unit output indicate the cash available for repayments and help phase spending on the three boutiques.
4. Unit cost can be checked as $240,000 ÷ 20,000 = $12 plus $18 variable cost = $30 a garment, allowing VVB to benchmark whether 14% labour turnover and the 38 stock complaints are pushing costs above target each quarter.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 8,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $30 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: 12,000-unit margin of safety against 20,000 output; discount pricing from $48 using $30 contribution; servicing the $200,000 loan and $560,000 refurbishment; and unit-cost benchmarking at $30 against turnover and stock complaints.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate VVB's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has VVB's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.95 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 2.10 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.65 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.50 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $130,000 inventories + $25,000 trade receivables + $40,000 cash = $195,000; 2025 current assets = $160,000 + $20,000 + $30,000 = $210,000. Dividing by current liabilities gives 2024 $195,000 ÷ $100,000 = 1.95 and ($195,000 − $130,000) ÷ $100,000 = $65,000 ÷ $100,000 = 0.65. For 2025, $210,000 ÷ $100,000 = 2.10 and ($210,000 − $160,000) ÷ $100,000 = $50,000 ÷ $100,000 = 0.50.

Evaluation: The two measures give conflicting signals. The first rose from 1.95 to 2.10, but only because inventories climbed from $130,000 to $160,000 while cash fell from $40,000 to $30,000 and current liabilities stayed at $100,000. The second measure, which excludes stock, fell from 0.65 to 0.50, showing that VVB's liquid assets now cover a smaller share of its short-term debts. This matters for a boutique chain with $240,000 fixed costs, a $200,000 bank loan and a $560,000 refurbishment: the business is increasingly reliant on selling slow-moving clothing stock to meet bills, exactly when 38 complaints about unavailable sizes suggest the inventory mix is wrong. Trade receivables did improve, falling from $25,000 to $20,000, which releases a little cash, but it is not enough to offset the stock build-up.

Conclusion: VVB's financial position has not improved. Although the broader measure rose, the stock-free measure deteriorated from 0.65 to 0.50, so the apparent strength depends on inventories that may not convert to cash quickly. VVB should reduce stock levels and protect cash before committing further funds to the online store.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventories, receivables and liabilities and a justified conclusion on the financial position.

questions.question_text: VVB is launching an online store alongside its six boutiques. Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for VVB of this approach.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: An online store lets VVB reach the 49% of 900 surveyed shoppers who said they would shop online, extending sales beyond the six boutiques without the full cost of new premises. Extra garment sales would spread the $240,000 fixed costs and support the $30 contribution, helping the $560,000 refurbishment pay back sooner even if the 38 complaints about unavailable sizes continue in physical shops.

Disadvantage: Running an e-commerce operation needs website, payment and delivery systems that add costs and require new skills, while the workforce of 40 already suffers 14% labour turnover and 11 staff lack on-the-job training. The insert gives no figure for setup cost or online sales volume, so the net gain cannot be quantified and the decision rests on judgement. Elena Vale should pilot the online store in one region, tracking the 5,400-garment baseline and the 38 complaints before scaling up, and should not assume the 58% who value knowledgeable staff will transfer their loyalty online.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to VVB's survey, costs, turnover and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.0%, the 6.4% minimum wage increase and the 10.8% rise in wholesale clothing input costs will affect VVB. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.0%): If VVB's $200,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the extra 0.75 percentage point adds 0.75% × $200,000 = $1,500 a year (0.0075 × $200,000). That is modest beside fixed costs of $240,000, and a fixed-rate loan would avoid it entirely. The rise could make future borrowing dearer and might slightly slow the 2.6% growth in fashion spending.

Minimum wage increase (6.4%, to $13.94 an hour): VVB's workforce of 40 includes many hourly-paid sales assistants, so payroll rises and cannot be avoided, particularly with 14% labour turnover forcing repeated hiring. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so any annual total would be invented. The defensible check is productivity: 20,000 units ÷ 40 staff = 500 garments per worker, so the higher wage is affordable only if that rate holds or improves; training the 11 untrained staff and reducing turnover would help protect it.

Wholesale clothing input costs (10.8%): These feed the $18 variable cost on every garment. The insert does not decompose that cost, so only a bound is honest: if the full $18 were exposed, 10.8% × $18 = $1.944, about $1.94 a unit, and at 20,000 units that is roughly $38,880 a year (20,000 × $1.944). Even a smaller exposed share reduces the $30 contribution on each garment, and the effect repeats on every sale.

Conclusion: The 10.8% rise in wholesale clothing input costs will have the greatest impact. It compounds across all 20,000 garments and directly erodes the $30 contribution that services the $200,000 loan and funds the $560,000 refurbishment, whereas the interest rise costs only $1,500 a year and the wage effect can be offset by sustaining 500 garments per worker. VVB should tackle the 38 stock complaints and review the $48 price rather than absorb the whole increase.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to VVB.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on VVB's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in context with a well-justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.
